title.value: Temperature Distributions and Heating Efficiency of Oil Recovery By Hot Water Injection

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: A study was made to investigate the temperature behavior, and the controlling physical mechanisms, during hot water injection into and through a porous medium. Both experimental and mathematical studies have been made for flow in the axial direction in a cylindrical core with the heat losses into and through a surrounding medium in a radial direction. Experiments were made by injecting hot water at a constant injection rate and constant temperature into the porous medium. Temperatures during hot water injection were measured along both the axis and the wall of the tube. Both analytical and numerical formulations were made to approximate the experimental system. A short-time approximate solution was found for the analytical formulation of the model, and an explicit finite difference approach was used to simulate the model numerically. The results of the mathematical models were compared to the experimental measurements. On the whole, the agreement was reasonable, but the short-time solution yielded unrealistic vertical temperature profiles in describing the leading edge of the hotzone. Heating efficiency, i.e., the fraction of the cumulative heat injected which remains in the core, was obtained for both the experimental results and the results of the numerical solution. Experimental results showed that for a specified time of injection, low injection rates yielded higher heating efficiency values. On the other hand, for a given amount of hot water injected, the heating efficiency increased with the injection rate. This injection-rate dependence of heating efficiency did not agree with the rate-independent theoretical solution. The thermal properties of the injection interval and adjacent formation were evaluated by matching experimental temperature measurements with dimensionless plots of temperature rise vs. distance for various injection periods. From the results of modified type-curve matching for three different injection rates, the thermal conductivity of the surrounding formation was found to be a function of flow rate. This suggested that thermal conductivity in the radial direction in the injection interval was an important consideration and was perhaps a function of injection rate. Improvements in the heat model were suggested which included variation effective thermal conductivity with flow rate.
Ersoy, Demir. (1969). Temperature Distributions and Heating Efficiency of Oil Recovery By Hot Water Injection. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/nr482wq7321
